newsitem.title: USA: Occidental denies seeking Sudan sanctions waiver.
newsitem.headline: Occidental denies seeking Sudan sanctions waiver.

text.p: Occidental Oil and Gas Corp on Friday denied a report that it had sought any exemption from U.S. sanctions against Sudan.

"At no time did Occidental seek or receive any special exemption or special treatment of any kind from the U.S. government in connection with any potential projects in that country," Nathan Fagre, general counsel of Occidental Oil and Gas said in a letter to the Washington Post published Friday.

The Washington Post reported last month that to aid Occidental, which had been seeking a stake in a major oil field in Sudan, the Clinton administration had eased a law barring transactions between U.S. companies and countries accused of supporting terrorism.

"To the contrary, Occidental kept the U.S. government advised of its interest in Sudan for the very purpose of ensuring that any investments Occidental might make there would be in fully compliance with U.S. laws and policies," Fagre's letter said.

He said after Congress passed the anti-terrorism law last summer, the company asked the administration to state what its policy was on commercial investments in Sudan. The company was told policy would be settled in rules carrying out the law.

The regulations issued last August were designed to block deals that might help government-backed terrorists. But it allowed business deals to go ahead in Sudan and Syria while banning all business in Cuba, Iran, Iraq, Libya, and North Korea, against which Washington already had broad sanctions.
The company said it had "advised and consulted with" several U.S. agencies about its interest in Sudan.
"This is prudent business practice, consistent with long-standing Occidental policies, and there certainly is nothing wrong or improper about this type of exchange of information," Fagre wrote.
Up to now, Occidental has refused to make any public comment on its interest in Sudan.

Sudan recently signed two major oil production-sharing agreements, one with Canadian company Arakis Energy Corp, Malaysia's state oil company Petronas and China National Petroleum Corp, and one with Canadian firm International Petroleum Corp.

Occidental had been negotiating for a stake in the block with Arakis, but Sudan allegedly dropped the California-based company from the deal because it was annoyed with the United States for sending aid to states bordering Sudan.

Occidental had been rumored to be in serious discussions with IPC for the block that was awarded Thursday. IPC went so far as to say in its recently released annual report that it had a 50-50 agreement in place with a major U.S. company.
One source close to the deal said Occidental was involved with IPC until January 28, five days after the front-page story ran in the Washington Post.
